subject: convergence / prior for finite mixture growth model

messages.author: fc3bcfccab6afa5d
messages.subject: convergence / prior for finite mixture growth model
parts:
Dear stan users,

I recently started using STAN hoping it may help obtaining reasonably fast convergence for a mixture growth model compared to using JAGS.

This model aims at estimating the proportion of 1, 2 and 3+ years old fish and their corresponding weight from weight at capture data. I implemented a Von Bertalanffy growth model as a guide to how mean weights change with increasing age. I did not want to go for a broken stick approach as my goal will be to make this model hierarchical later on. Error on weight is assumed gamma (best option so far to get realistic weight estimates together with allowing the variance to be proportional to the mean).


I tend to run 3 chains and I usually get:

  •   2 chains with mean weights about 2, 4 and 6 kg and proportion of ages about 0.70, 0.25, 0.05 for ages 1, 2 and 3 respectively. This is quite realistic biologically.
  •   1 chain stuck with values of .7, 2.2 and 4.5 for mean weights and proportions of 0, .7 and .3. This gives reasonable fit to the data but it is clearly not realistic ecologically and the Log posterior values distribution associated is significantly lower than is the previous case.

This happens with giving rather informative starting values to the different chains. I thus wonder if I could improve things using different priors. I have the feeling that this could be the issue but any other suggestion you may have would also be very welcome.

If you have hints about how to change the code to make it faster that would be great too.


My R and Stan codes are provided below and a subset of the data is attached


Thanks in advance for your help.


Best


Guillaume


Stan model

Enter code here...
data {
  int<lower=0> n_fish; // number of fish
  int<lower=1> n_ages; // number of age classes in the model
  real<lower=0> weight[n_fish]; // weight of fish
}

parameters {
  real<lower=7500> weight_inf; // asymptotic weight
  real<lower=0.1> k; // growth rate
  real t_zero; // curve shifting
  real<lower=1.5> b; // weight length exponent factor
  real<lower=0> beta; // component of gamma likelyhood
  simplex[n_ages] p_ages; // age proportions, ie mixture
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower = 0> mu_weight_ages[n_ages]; // mean weight of an age class 
  real<lower = 0> alpha_ages[n_ages]; // component gamma likelyhood
  for(a in 1:n_ages){
   // Von Bertalanffy growth equation
   mu_weight_ages[a] = weight_inf * pow(1 - exp(-k * (a - t_zero)), b);
   alpha_ages[a] = mu_weight_ages[a] * beta;
  }
}

model {   
  real ps[n_ages];
  weight_inf ~ normal(30000, 3000);
  k ~ cauchy(0, 1);
  t_zero ~ normal(0, 1); 
  b ~ normal(2.84, 0.2); # informative prior
  beta ~ cauchy(0, 1);
  for(f in 1:n_fish){
      for(a in 1:n_ages){
          ps[a] = log(p_ages[a]) + gamma_lpdf(weight[f] |alpha_ages[a], beta);
      }
      target += log_sum_exp(ps);
  }  
}

R code
rm(list = ls())

setwd("C:/Users/gbal/Desktop/stan.users/")

require(rstan)
require(shinystan) # allows model post checking in firefox
require(coda)

#execution on a local, multicore CPU with excess RAM we recommend
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

###---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### check  and compile model or load stan file

model.name <- 'mixture.growth.model.gamma'
compiled.file.name <- paste0(model.name, '.cpp.RData')

# if new model tested
# file.remove(compiled.file.name)
# file.remove(paste0(model.name, '.rds'))

if(file.exists(compiled.file.name)){
  load(compiled.file.name) 
}else{
  assign(paste0('compiled.', model.name),
         stan_model(paste0(model.name, '.stan'))
  )
  save(list = paste0('compiled.',model.name), file = compiled.file.name)
}

###---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### load base weight data and get number fish

load('weight.data.subset.RData')

n_fish <- length(weight)

###---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### stan bits

# size of finite, user choice, 3 meaningfull biologically
n_ages <- 3

# stan data list
fish_dat <- list(n_fish = n_fish,
                 n_ages = n_ages,
                 weight = weight)

# inits chains
inits_model<-function(){
  list(
    'weight_inf' = abs(rnorm(1, mean = 30000, sd = 5000)),
    'k' = abs(rnorm(1, mean = 0.2, sd = 0.01)),
    'beta' = runif(1, 0.001, 0.01)
  )
}

# stan sampling
stan.fit <- sampling(get(paste0('compiled.', model.name)),
                     data = fish_dat,
                     warmup = 1000,
                     #thin = 1,
                     iter = 3000,
                     chains = 3,
                     #verbose = FALSE,
                     refresh = 150,
                     init = inits_model#,
                     #control = list('adapt_delta' = 0.85)
)

# shiny check results
launch_shinystan(stan.fit)

parts: See inline.

> On Mar 14, 2017, at 11:06 AM, Guillaume Bal <guillaum...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear stan users,
>
> I recently started using STAN hoping it may help obtaining reasonably fast convergence for a mixture growth model compared to using JAGS.
>
> This model aims at estimating the proportion of 1, 2 and 3+ years old fish and their corresponding weight from weight at capture data. I implemented a Von Bertalanffy growth model as a guide to how mean weights change with increasing age. I did not want to go for a broken stick approach as my goal will be to make this model hierarchical later on. Error on weight is assumed gamma (best option so far to get realistic weight estimates together with allowing the variance to be proportional to the mean).
>
>
>
> I tend to run 3 chains and I usually get:
>
> • 2 chains with mean weights about 2, 4 and 6 kg and proportion of ages about 0.70, 0.25, 0.05 for ages 1, 2 and 3 respectively. This is quite realistic biologically.
> • 1 chain stuck with values of .7, 2.2 and 4.5 for mean weights and proportions of 0, .7 and .3. This gives reasonable fit to the data but it is clearly not realistic ecologically and the Log posterior values distribution associated is significantly lower than is the previous case.

Michael just wrote a case study on mixture models:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/identifying_mixture_models.html

The problem is that you can't jump between the modes you're
finding.

If you start near the solution you want and keep the initial
step size low, it'll be less likely to randomly jump away to start.

This is only going to be kosher if you know the probabiliy mass
around the other mode is low (it can be high with low density values
if it covers a lot of raw Euclidean volume).
> This happens with giving rather informative starting values to the different chains. I thus wonder if I could improve things using different priors.

A prior that avoids the weights going to zero might
help. Something like

p_ages ~ dirichlet(alpha_p_ages);

where alpha_p_ages is rep_vector(a, K) where K is the size
of p_ages and a >> 1.

> I have the feeling that this could be the issue but any other suggestion you may have would also be very welcome.
>
> If you have hints about how to change the code to make it faster that would be great too.
See below.

>
>
> Enter code here...
> data {
> int<lower=0> n_fish; // number of fish
> int<lower=1> n_ages; // number of age classes in the model
> real<lower=0> weight[n_fish]; // weight of fish
> }
>
> parameters {
> real<lower=7500> weight_inf; // asymptotic weight

We don't recommend these hard cutoffs, but recommend priors.
It's a big problem if you wind up with mass near the boundaries.

Also, keeping params unit scale will help. For example, take
the parameter to be

real<lower=0> weight_raw;

and then scale it manually as a transformed parameter:

weight_inf = 7500 * weight_raw;
> real<lower=0.1> k; // growth rate
Same comment.

> real t_zero; // curve shifting
> real<lower=1.5> b; // weight length exponent factor
Same comment.

> real<lower=0> beta; // component of gamma likelyhood
> simplex[n_ages] p_ages; // age proportions, ie mixture
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
> real<lower = 0> mu_weight_ages[n_ages]; // mean weight of an age class
> real<lower = 0> alpha_ages[n_ages]; // component gamma likelyhood
> for(a in 1:n_ages){
> // Von Bertalanffy growth equation
> mu_weight_ages[a] = weight_inf * pow(1 - exp(-k * (a - t_zero)), b);
This can be unstable with exp inside of pow, especially if b is large.
> alpha_ages[a] = mu_weight_ages[a] * beta;
Vectorize this.

> }
> }
>
> model {
> real ps[n_ages];
> weight_inf ~ normal(30000, 3000);

weight_inf_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

weight_inf = 30000 + weight_inf_raw * 3000;

> k ~ cauchy(0, 1);
> t_zero ~ normal(0, 1);
> b ~ normal(2.84, 0.2); # informative prior
> beta ~ cauchy(0, 1);

The Cauchy's can be too fat---see how far beta and k are moving
out into the tails.

> for(f in 1:n_fish){
> for(a in 1:n_ages){
> ps[a] = log(p_ages[a]) + gamma_lpdf(weight[f] |alpha_ages[a], beta);

Precomputing and saving log(p_ages) will save recomputing it.

> }
> target += log_sum_exp(ps);
> }
> }
>

- Bob

Dear Bob and Michael,

First thanks a lot for your answers. I really appreciate them and I am going to try them out very soon.

In particular, I'll vectorize the code a bit mode, will use more informative priors when possible and try to get the scale units comparable.

Here are a few more elements/ question following your comments:
 - I get the idea that starting near the 'right answer' lead to small jumps. Just for my information, is there a way to increase the jump size ? 
   I guess it is probably possible to do it through arguments within control but it is a bit obscure to me.
-  about the two kind of convergence I mentioned, the second one, tending to go toward a binomial mixture, is not 'a complete aberration' ecologically speaking.
   Nonetheless according to expert knowledge, it is sub-optimal and that does reflect on the lp__ values as well.  
 - About the cauchy being to fat, do you mean to much of a tail ? If yes I think it might be right. Indeed the k and beta posteriors are centered on 0.18 (sd =  0.01) and  3.3e-03(sd =2.4 e-4). 
   A tighter prior may be better and maybe going for a half normal would also improve things.
 - I looked at your link and I think the model I wrote should be alright as the growth model implies some ordering
 - about the problem with the power factor, there is quite on informative prior centered on 2.84. I guess this should limit the issue you mentioned 
  
Let me know if I got you right and thanks again for your time

Guillaume

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] convergence / prior for finite mixture growth model
parts:
> On Mar 16, 2017, at 10:38 AM, Guillaume Bal <guillaum...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob and Michael,
>
> First thanks a lot for your answers. I really appreciate them and I am going to try them out very soon.
>
> In particular, I'll vectorize the code a bit mode, will use more informative priors when possible and try to get the scale units comparable.
>
> Here are a few more elements/ question following your comments:
> - I get the idea that starting near the 'right answer' lead to small jumps. Just for my information, is there a way to increase the jump size ?
> I guess it is probably possible to do it through arguments within control but it is a bit obscure to me.

stepsize sets initial step size and adapt_delta gives you target acceptance
rate---closer to 1 that is, the smaller the stepsize required. Or you can
just fix it, but then you need to use a default mass matrix until a release or
two from now.
> - about the two kind of convergence I mentioned, the second one, tending to go toward a binomial mixture, is not 'a complete aberration' ecologically speaking.

Then the model's wrong if it has way less probability mass
than the other mode (with three components).
> Nonetheless according to expert knowledge, it is sub-optimal and that does reflect on the lp__ values as well.

The lp__ values are about density---what you care about is
probability mass, which is density integrated over a volume.
> - About the cauchy being to fat, do you mean to much of a tail ?
Yes.

> If yes I think it might be right. Indeed the k and beta posteriors are centered on 0.18 (sd = 0.01) and 3.3e-03(sd =2.4 e-4).
> A tighter prior may be better and maybe going for a half normal would also improve things.

> - I looked at your link and I think the model I wrote should be alright as the growth model implies some ordering
> - about the problem with the power factor, there is quite on informative prior centered on 2.84. I guess this should limit the issue you mentioned

It can still be easy to fall into a mode and not escape if
the density in between the modes is too low. You can try
initializing around the mode you know is right and starting
stepsize low. You'll get the right answer if and only if
there's roughly no probability mass in the other modes (again,
I want to stress this is mass, not density).

- Bob
